subtype: Approach: verify AI outputs against reliable sources [Action]
passage:
Selin pasted a summary of a research paper into her notes, and it read beautifully: one clear claim, a percentage, and two citations. Before using it in her seminar talk, she made a small list. One: find the paper. Two: read the abstract and the results table. Three: look for the percentage. Four: search for each citation.

From her flat in Istanbul, she opened the original on her laptop. The percentage was close but not the same, and the paper said "in a small sample," which the summary had dropped. One of the citations did not exist at all.

She corrected the number, added the caveat, and sent her friend Sofia a quick message: "Glad I checked. Never trusting a tidy summary again."

qa.q: How many citations did the summary give, and how many turned out not to exist?
qa.a: The summary gave two citations, and one of them did not exist at all.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when she saw the citation did not exist?
qa.a: Selin was surprised and relieved, since the check had caught an error before it reached her talk.

qa.q: What could Selin do next time she wants a quick overview, and why?
qa.a: Selin could use the summary only as a map and read the original paper's abstract and results herself, because a tidy summary can be wrong while still sounding sure.

qa.q: How might Sofia see Selin's message?
qa.a: Sofia may feel the lesson is useful for Sofia's own work and admire the care Selin took before speaking to the seminar.

grounding: Before using an AI summary, the person checks the claims and citations against the original paper.

passage:
The second-floor reading room of the college library was nearly empty when Neelam spread out her seminar notes. The chatbot's summary of the paper looked perfect: a sample of 400 teenagers, a strong link between sleep and grades, and two supporting studies.
"Are you just using that?" Noor asked, sliding into the next chair.
"Not yet." Neelam opened the original PDF beside the summary and went line by line. Step one: the sample. The paper said 240, not 400. Step two: the main finding. The paper called the link "modest", not strong. Step three: the citations. One study was real. The other, with a neat title and author, didn't exist anywhere in the library database.
It took an extra hour. Her slides ended up plainer, but when the professor asked about the sample, Neelam gave the right number.

qa.q: What sample size did the original paper actually report?
How did Neelam feel when Noor asked if she was just using the summary?
qa.a: Neelam felt cautious and not ready to trust it, which is why the answer was 'Not yet' before checking the original.

qa.q: What else could Neelam do next time to save that extra hour?
qa.a: She could read the paper's abstract and results herself first, then use the summary only as a guide to check, since she already knows what to look for.

qa.q: How might the checking affect the rest of the seminar class?
qa.a: Classmates hear accurate numbers and a real citation, so they do not carry a made-up study into their own notes.

grounding: Shows the person checking a tool's summary claims and citations against the original paper before using it, finding confident but wrong statements.

subtype: Approach: verify AI outputs against reliable sources [Action]
passage:
Hi Swati,
Before I paste anything into our group literature review, here's what I checked this morning.
The chatbot summarised the cycle-lane paper as saying new lanes "cut commute times by 30 percent across the city." I opened the paper itself. Page 6 says the 30 percent drop was only for trips under 5 kilometres, and only in two neighbourhoods.
Then I looked up its two citations. The first one is real and matches. The second, "Laurent and Obi, 2020", doesn't appear in any journal I can find, including the library's search.
So I've rewritten our paragraph using only what the paper says, with page numbers, and I've marked the fake citation in red in our shared file so nobody reuses it.
Can you check my paragraph before Friday's meeting?
Karthik

qa.q: How far did trips have to be for the 30 percent drop to apply?
qa.a: The drop was only for trips under 5 kilometres, and only in two neighbourhoods.

qa.q: What does Karthik's red marking suggest Karthik is worried about?
qa.a: Karthik seems wary and a bit alarmed that someone in the group could reuse a made-up citation without noticing.

qa.q: What other habit could the group adopt, and why?
qa.a: The group could agree that every claim in the review carries a page number from the original source, so unchecked tool summaries cannot slip in.

qa.q: How might Swati feel reading this email?
qa.a: Swati might feel relieved and reassured, since the review now rests on the actual paper and the fake source is flagged.

grounding: Shows the person verifying a tool's summary and citations against the original paper before using them, because the tool stated wrong things confidently.
